title: In the Matter of DoNotPay, Inc. — FTC Decision and Order, Complaint, and final-order announcement (Matter No. 2323042)
author: Federal Trade Commission

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The FTC matter accepts the cluster’s core distinction between bounded AI functionality and general legal competence, grounding it in a concrete enforcement case involving absent capability testing, limited expert verification and unusable outputs. It materially extends the synthesis by imposing binding substantiation, evidence-preservation, reporting and monitoring duties for professional-performance claims.
qs: DoNotPay did not test whether the Service’s law-related features operated like a human lawyer.

kp.k: FTC settlement addresses deceptive AI substitution claims
kp.d: The FTC charged DoNotPay with false or unsubstantiated human-lawyer performance claims and false claims about website diagnostics and subscription features under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. This is a consent settlement, not an admission by DoNotPay that the substantive allegations were true: the Commission found reason to believe a violation occurred, while DoNotPay neither admitted nor denied the allegations except jurisdictional facts for this action. The final-order announcement is dated February 11, 2025.
qs: The acts and practices of the Respondent as alleged in this complaint constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce in violation of Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act.
it neither admits nor denies any of the allegations in the Complaint, except as specifically stated in this Decision and Order

kp.k: DoNotPay marketed consumer-facing AI as replacing lawyers
kp.d: The complaint describes an online subscription service for U.S. consumers dealing with commercial issues and American civil law. Its challenged positioning was substitution for legal expertise, rather than assistance to a supervising lawyer: the FTC reports that its CEO sought to replace the legal industry. Advertised tasks included demand letters, contracts, small-claims complaints, traffic-ticket challenges and parking-ticket appeals. These are reported company representations, not FTC findings that AI could perform those tasks adequately.
qs: The DoNotPay Service is an online subscription service targeted to U.S. consumers seeking assistance with a range of commercial issues and legal issues involving American civil law.

The Chief Executive Officer for DoNotPay has claimed that the company’s goals were “to be like the general counsel for the consumer,” and “to replace the $200-billion-dollar legal industry with artificial intelligence.”

kp.k: Subscriptions promised tailored expertise at consumer price points
kp.d: According to the complaint, General Membership had been offered since 2019 and, at relevant times, cost $36 every two months; the Small Business Protection Plan had been offered since 2021 and, at relevant times, cost $49.99 per month. Prices fluctuated. The challenged legal-service promise went beyond document production to applying relevant law to individual circumstances and avoiding complications involving limitation periods, compensation limits and jurisdiction. The FTC alleged that the service was not designed to operate like a lawyer in these respects.
qs: Respondent charged subscribers $36 every two months.
Respondent charged subscribers $49.99 per month.
In fact, the DoNotPay Service was not designed to operate like a human lawyer in these respects.

kp.k: FTC alleged absent testing and attorney quality evaluation
kp.d: The complaint identifies natural language processing, chatbot software and an API with OpenAI’s ChatGPT among the service’s technologies. It alleges that none was trained on a comprehensive, current corpus of federal and state law or its application to fact patterns; most law-related features had not undergone employee testing for output quality and accuracy, and attorneys had not been employed or retained to test them. These are allegations about substantiation and product evaluation, not measured model error rates or evidence about all legal AI.
qs: DoNotPay did not test whether the Service’s law-related features operated like a human lawyer.

None of the Service’s technologies has been trained on a comprehensive and current corpus of federal and state laws, regulations, and judicial decisions or on the application of those laws to fact patterns.
DoNotPay employees have not tested the quality and accuracy of the legal documents and advice generated by most of the Service’s law-related features.

kp.k: Limited fact collection undermined claimed individualized legal assistance
kp.d: The FTC illustrates its allegations with the assault-related “Sue Now” workflow: it requested a short incident description, returned the same irrelevant response to additional questions or concerns, and generated a half-page demand letter. The complaint also reports subscriber complaints about omitted relevant facts, overlooked legal issues and unusable documents. It gives no complaint count, representative sample or quantified failure rate.
qs: The Service elicited few facts from subscribers utilizing the law-related features described in paragraphs 12 through 18, above.

The Service then would have generated a half-page demand letter with a phrase-length description of the incident, a monetary demand, and a warning that failure to settle could result in a costly legal judgment.

DoNotPay subscribers who used the law-related features have complained that the Service did not ask them to submit information relevant to their breach of contract claims, failed to consider important legal issues, and generated legal documents that were not fit for use.

kp.k: Website diagnostics and feature availability attracted separate allegations
kp.d: The complaint alleges that DoNotPay promoted detecting hundreds of federal and state law violations on a small-business website using only an email address, invoking potential legal fees of $125,000, but did not perform the advertised analysis. It separately alleges that General Membership advertised unavailable copyright-protection, defamation-letter, non-compete and residential-lease features. The order prohibits misrepresentations about document or website analysis, legal-fee savings and purchased features.
qs: This feature purportedly would detect legal violations that, if unaddressed, would potentially cost a consumer $125,000 in legal fees.
DoNotPay’s website diagnostic tool did not, in fact, analyze a consumer’s small business website for hundreds of federal and state law violations based solely on an email address.

At times relevant to this Complaint, DoNotPay’s website advertised that a General Membership included features that could protect a copyright and generate a customized cease- and-desist letter for a defamation claim, non-compete agreement, and residential lease when those features were not available.

kp.k: Professional-equivalence advertising requires reliable supporting evidence
kp.d: The order conditions human-lawyer and other performance representations on their being non-misleading and supported, when made, by competent and reliable evidence sufficient under generally accepted standards in the relevant field. Such evidence must draw on relevant professional expertise and objective evaluation by qualified persons. The restriction is conditional, not a categorical prohibition on AI legal services or on all lawyer-equivalence claims.
qs: at the time such representation is made, they possess and rely upon competent and reliable evidence
to substantiate that the representation is true.
have been conducted and evaluated in an objective manner by qualified persons
are generally accepted in the profession to yield accurate and reliable results.

kp.k: Order extends beyond legal services to professional-service products
kp.d: The order covers the DoNotPay Service and other internet-enabled products or services that DoNotPay directly or indirectly controls or operates and that purportedly provide professional services. Its substantiation requirement therefore reaches claims of equivalence to professionals in other fields, not only lawyers. The definition expressly includes accounting, engineering, consulting, education and medical services, among others; these are the order’s scope, not evidence that DoNotPay actually supplied each service.
qs: “Covered Product or Service” means the DoNotPay Service and any other Internet- enabled product or service controlled or operated, directly or indirectly, by Respondent that purportedly provides Professional Services.
including that the Covered Product or Service performs a Professional Service like a professional in the relevant field

kp.k: California unauthorized-practice concerns accompanied federal advertising enforcement
kp.d: The FTC complaint reports that the California Bar opened an unauthorized-practice investigation on or about November 16, 2021. It alleges that DoNotPay continued robot-lawyer representations after its CEO promised on or about January 21, 2022 to stop, and continued robot-lawyer and “sue anyone” promotion despite assurances of removal following a June 15, 2023 cease-and-desist notice. These are reported state-bar allegations and company conduct within the FTC complaint, not an FTC adjudication of unauthorized practice.
qs: On or about November 16, 2021, the Office of Chief Trial Counsel of the State Bar of California (“the California Bar”) opened an investigation into the DoNotPay Service related to allegations of engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
On June 15, 2023, the California Bar sent a cease-and-desist notice alleging the DoNotPay Service amounted to engagement in the unauthorized practice of law.

Notwithstanding these representations to the California Bar, the DoNotPay website and social media account continued to promote the Service as the “World’s First Robot Lawyer” and advertise “sue anyone” claims.

kp.k: Settlement imposes monetary relief and corrective customer notices
kp.d: The order requires $193,000 in monetary relief and identification of new subscribers between January 1, 2021 and December 31, 2023, with email notification to identified eligible customers whose email addresses are held. Its prescribed notice explains that lawyer-equivalence claims lacked sufficient proof and must not recur without adequate evidence. Funds may support consumer redress and related relief; the document does not establish that every subscriber will receive a refund.
qs: Respondent must pay to the Commission one-hundred-ninety-three-thousand dollars ($193,000.00)
Respondent must identify all new subscribers to the DoNotPay Service between January 1, 2021 and December 31, 2023 (“eligible customers”).

Unless we have sufficient evidence to back up our claims, we can’t advertise that DoNotPay acts like a real lawyer by, for example, writing legal demand letters, filing cases in small claims court, or giving legal advice.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The FTC alleges that DoNotPay marketed automated legal assistance as a substitute for human legal expertise without delivering or substantiating the advertised capabilities.
pts.d: The FTC's claim concerns this service, not the capabilities of all legal AI. The complaint distinguishes document generation from applying law to individual facts and anticipating limitations periods, jurisdictional issues and compensation limits. It characterizes DoNotPay's lawyer-equivalence representations as false, misleading or unsubstantiated. This is a consent resolution: DoNotPay neither admitted nor denied the allegations, apart from jurisdictional admissions. The company's ambition to replace the legal industry is reported as challenged marketing context, not adopted as an FTC prediction.

pts.k: The FTC also alleges that advertised automated website compliance analysis, associated legal-fee savings and some subscription features were not actually available or achievable as represented.
pts.d: The website diagnostic claim concerned detecting hundreds of federal and state legal violations from an email address and avoiding substantial potential legal fees. Separately, the complaint alleges that advertised copyright protection and certain customized legal-document features were unavailable at relevant times. These are allegations about product functionality and consumer advertising, not measured estimates of AI-driven savings.

pts.k: The final order conditions DoNotPay's future lawyer-equivalence and professional-performance advertising on non-misleading claims supported by competent and reliable evidence.
pts.d: The operative regulatory consequence is a substantiation requirement, not a categorical ban on AI legal services or a finding that AI can never perform lawyer-like tasks. It applies to DoNotPay and the persons covered by the order, including covered Internet-enabled professional-service products it controls or operates. The order separately prohibits misrepresenting legal-fee savings, document-analysis abilities and included features. It requires $193,000 in monetary relief and customer notification. The FTC proceeding concerns deceptive practices under Section 5; the complaint separately recounts California Bar unauthorized-practice allegations, rather than deciding those allegations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The FTC supports its allegations with advertising exhibits, descriptions of service behavior, asserted deficiencies in testing and legal expertise, and subscriber complaints.
pts.d: Complaint paragraphs 19–21 describe sparse factual intake, a generic response to additional questions and a half-page demand letter in the assault workflow. They allege no lawyer-equivalence testing, no attorney testing and no quality-and-accuracy testing by employees for most law-related features. The complaint also describes limitations in the technologies' training. These are investigative allegations, not a published comparative benchmark, quantified error rate or representative outcome study. The purported newspaper endorsement is traced to a high-school student's opinion piece rather than presented as independent professional validation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source addresses historical marketing and service performance, followed by ongoing advertising conditions; it supplies no forecast of when AI will replace lawyers.
pts.d: General Membership began in 2019 and the Small Business Protection Plan in 2021. Advertising exhibits include captures from 2023 and April 2024. The complaint was announced in September 2024; the final-order announcement is dated February 11, 2025. The supplied documents contain a dating discrepancy: the decision and complaint state January 14, 2025, while the press release reports an approval vote on January 16. The order becomes effective on website publication as a final order and generally lasts 20 years from issuance, subject to its enforcement-extension provisions. Substantiation must exist when a representation is made. Notification covers identified new subscribers from January 1, 2021 through December 31, 2023, with initial notices due within 180 days of issuance and later identifications subject to additional deadlines.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are US individual consumers and small-business subscribers seeking direct legal help, and DoNotPay as the regulated provider.
pts.d: The service targeted civil-law and consumer matters, including demand letters, contracts, small-claims filings, family-related documents and ticket challenges. The challenged model offered consumers direct reliance on automated outputs in place of hiring a lawyer, rather than a lawyer-supervised copilot. Small businesses were targeted with website-compliance and legal-fee-avoidance claims. Subscribers were allegedly exposed to unsuitable documents or unavailable features; eligible past subscribers must receive settlement notices, and the monetary relief may support consumer redress. The source does not quantify effects on lawyer employment, law-firm economics or the civil justice gap.
